How Quantum Physics, Human Cognition, and Artificial Intelligence Converged on the Same Geometry

1. The Pedagogical Lie We Tell About Physics
There is a story about physics that nearly every student encounters, a clean and satisfying narrative in which the history of science divides neatly into three grand chapters. The first belongs to Newton: a universe of absolute space and time, of billiard balls following determinate trajectories, of forces transmitted across distances and futures calculated with clockwork precision. The second belongs to Einstein: a universe in which space and time are not the fixed stage on which events play out but are themselves part of the drama, warped by mass and energy, relative to the observer, woven into a four-dimensional fabric that curves and bends and tells matter how to move. The third belongs to the stranger figures of the early twentieth century — Bohr, Heisenberg, Dirac, Schrödinger, and the mathematician John von Neumann, whose rigorous reformulation of quantum mechanics in terms of Hilbert spaces turned out, improbably, to be the language in which nature reveals its deepest secrets. In this third chapter, certainty dissolves into probability, particles refuse to have definite positions until you look at them, and the act of measurement becomes not a passive reading of pre-existing facts but an irreducible participation in the constitution of reality.
This is a beautiful story, it even has a neat, three-act structure to it, and like many beautiful stories told to beginners, it is substantially false.
The falseness is not in the details. Each of those frameworks is real, mathematically precise, and extraordinarily well-confirmed by experiment. The falseness is in the architecture of the narrative itself, in the implicit suggestion that these three paradigms carve nature at its joints — that they describe separate territories of reality, divided by scale, each sovereign within its own domain. Classical mechanics for the human-sized world of baseballs and bridges. Relativity for the cosmic world of black holes and the expanding universe. Quantum theory for the subatomic world of electrons and photons. This is the map that gets drawn in textbooks, and it is, at the level of pedagogy, defensible. It helps students build intuitions before confronting the deeper picture. But it installs a conceptual error that is surprisingly hard to dislodge, and that error matters enormously once we try to think clearly about the relationship between physics, mind, and the mathematics of intelligence.
The error is this: these paradigms do not correspond to different sizes of things. They correspond to different levels of description, separated not by scale but by how much information we choose to throw away.
To understand what this means, it helps to start with the physicist Sean Carroll’s blunt and deliberately unsettling claim: the universe is quantum. Not “quantum at small scales” and classical everywhere else. Not “quantum in the laboratory and Newtonian in the street.” Quantum, full stop, as a statement about what fundamentally exists. The electrons in your neurons, the carbon atoms in your bones, the gravitational field that keeps you in your chair — all of it is, at the deepest level we can currently describe, quantum mechanical. There is no non-quantum realm hiding somewhere beneath the macroscopic world, upholding its classical behavior. There is only the quantum world, and the classical world that emerges from it under certain conditions.
Those conditions are what make all the difference, and they are worth understanding precisely, because they form the conceptual foundation for everything that follows in this chapter and in this book.
Newtonian physics is not the physics of medium-sized objects. It is an effective description of systems in which three conditions are approximately satisfied: velocities are much smaller than the speed of light, the relevant scales of action are enormously larger than Planck’s constant, and quantum coherence — the fragile property that allows quantum systems to exist in superpositions of multiple states simultaneously — has been destroyed by interaction with the environment. When those conditions hold, the full machinery of quantum mechanics simplifies dramatically. Wave functions collapse into definite trajectories. Probabilities sharpen into certainties. The strange non-locality and contextuality of quantum systems vanish behind a curtain of apparent classical determinism. You can treat a baseball as having a definite position and momentum at every moment, not because it fundamentally does — it doesn’t — but because the quantum uncertainty in its position is so astronomically small relative to any measurement you could make that it is operationally irrelevant. Newtonian mechanics is not a separate theory operating in a separate domain. It is quantum mechanics with its eyes closed to detail.
The situation with relativity is subtler, and it is here that the standard pedagogical story most seriously misleads. Relativity, in the textbook account, is the physics of the very large and the very fast: galaxies, black holes, spacetime curvature, GPS satellites that need relativistic corrections. Quantum mechanics, by contrast, is the physics of the very small: atoms, electrons, the behavior of matter at scales where Planck’s constant becomes relevant. The two frameworks are thus implicitly assigned to different size ranges, which creates the impression that they are in principle compatible with each other and that their current incompatibility at extreme scales is merely a technical problem awaiting a solution.
But this is wrong in an important way. Relativity does not belong only to the large scale. Relativistic effects matter wherever velocities, fields, or energies make them significant, including in atomic physics: for heavy atoms such as gold, inner-shell electrons are sufficiently relativistic that relativistic corrections are essential for explaining important chemical and physical properties. Particle accelerators operate entirely within relativistic regimes, and the particles they produce and destroy are described by quantum field theory, which is both fully quantum and fully relativistic. The Standard Model of particle physics — the most precisely tested theory in the history of science — is a relativistic quantum field theory, beginning with Dirac’s relativistic wave equation in the late 1920s and culminating in quantum field theories of the electromagnetic, weak, and strong forces. There is no fundamental conflict between quantum theory and special relativity in the domain described by relativistic quantum field theory, which successfully unifies them for nongravitational phenomena. The fault line runs elsewhere: between quantum theory and general relativity, specifically at the Planck scale where spacetime itself becomes subject to quantum fluctuations and our current mathematical tools break down entirely.
This matters because it forces a reordering of the conceptual hierarchy. The standard picture presents three parallel frameworks, each valid in its domain, each roughly co-equal in foundational status. The corrected picture is a nested structure in which quantum theory is not one framework among three but the underlying substrate from which the others emerge. General relativity, in this view, is not the fundamental theory of spacetime — it is an effective theory, a description of what spacetime looks like when you treat it as smooth and classical and ignore the quantum fluctuations operating at scales far below anything current experiments can probe. It is, in the technical language of modern physics, a classical limit of a deeper quantum gravitational theory that we do not yet have but are confident must exist. And Newtonian mechanics, in turn, is a further limit of general relativity, applicable when gravitational fields are weak and velocities are small.
The corrected hierarchy, then, runs in the opposite direction from the one most people learn. It is not Newton, then Einstein, then quantum, arranged as three successive revelations of increasing strangeness. It is quantum at the foundation, from which spacetime emerges through coarse-graining, from which general relativity emerges as the effective theory of that spacetime, from which Newtonian mechanics emerges as a further approximation when fields are weak and speeds are low. Each step in this sequence involves a systematic throwing-away of information — a process physicists call coarse-graining — in which the fine-grained quantum details are averaged over, phase relations are destroyed, and what remains is a simplified effective description that is perfectly adequate for the purposes at hand but is not the whole story.
Coarse-graining is not a minor technical footnote. It is the conceptual key to understanding how very different-looking descriptions of the world can all be true simultaneously without contradicting each other. When you replace the quantum description of a gas — a description involving the quantum states of something on the order of ten to the twenty-third particles, their entanglement relations, their individual positions and momenta represented as probability amplitudes — with a thermodynamic description involving temperature, pressure, and volume, you have not changed the gas. You have changed the description. You have chosen to track certain large-scale collective variables and to deliberately ignore the microscopic details whose complexity vastly exceeds any practical purpose. The temperature of a gas is not a fundamental feature of reality in the way that the quantum state of its constituent particles might be. It is a coarse-grained variable, a statistical summary of an underlying quantum reality that has been blurred by your choice of what to measure and what to ignore.
The same logic applies to spacetime itself, and this is where modern theoretical physics has arrived at one of its most striking and still-contested propositions: that space and time are not fundamental. They are emergent. Spacetime, in this view, is what you get when you coarse-grain quantum entanglement structure at a particular scale. The smooth, continuous, curved geometry that Einstein’s equations describe is not the bedrock of physical reality but a large-scale pattern arising from a more fundamental quantum substrate, in something like the way that temperature arises from molecular motion or the hardness of a table top arises from quantum mechanical repulsion between electron clouds. If this is right — and an increasing number of serious theoretical physicists believe it is at least directionally correct, even if the precise mechanism remains unknown — then “small” and “large” are not fundamental categories. They are categories defined within spacetime, and spacetime is itself emergent. The distinction between the very small (where quantum effects are obvious) and the very large (where classical behavior seems to reign) is a distinction that only makes sense within the emergent picture, not at the level of the fundamental reality from which that picture arises.
Why does any of this matter for a chapter about mind, meaning, and artificial intelligence?
It matters because once you understand the physics correctly, you discover that what seemed like three separate mathematical frameworks are actually three levels of approximation to a single underlying mathematical structure. And that structure — the mathematics of quantum theory, the mathematics of Hilbert spaces and linear operators and inner products and high-dimensional vector spaces — turns out to be not merely the language of subatomic physics but something far more general and far more strange.
